headline: mixed
texts: Some of this topic is solid and some is not yet. Perforated ulcer is mostly a set of qualifiers: most common versus always, first versus best, sealed versus free. The objectives below show which qualifiers slipped. Start the review cards with the ones marked as gaps.
Site and wall-to-outcome are partly there. Anchor it: the anterior wall faces the free peritoneal cavity, the posterior wall faces the gastroduodenal artery. Revisit the O1 card.
Free gas versus Chilaiditi is only partly secure. Check haustra and the patient, not just the location under the dome. Redo the O2 card.
The clinical picture is partly secure. Trace the sequence once more: chemical peritonitis, apparent improvement, then bacterial peritonitis. Redo the O3 card.
First versus most sensitive test is partly secure. Name which question the stem asks before choosing. Redo the O4 card.
What a clear film or soft abdomen excludes is partly secure. Neither rules perforation out, and a quarter of films show no gas. Redo the O5 card.
View, timing and contrast are partly secure. Derive each from the mechanism: where gas rises, how long it takes, what leaks into the peritoneum. Redo the O6 card.
The order of care in a shocked patient is partly secure. Ask what keeps the patient alive to reach anaesthesia. Redo the O7 card.
The operation and patch names are partly secure. Graham is a free plug and Cellan-Jones a pedicled tongue, though PYQs key 'Graham's patch'. Redo the O8 card.
Post-repair care and the gastric addition are partly secure. Recheck the modern logic and remember the biopsy step for gastric ulcers. Redo the O9 card.
When Taylor management applies is partly secure. The qualifier is sealed, confirmed on Gastrografin, and stable. Redo the O10 card.
The Boey score is partly secure. Rebuild three items: shock (systolic under 100), major illness, delay over 24 hours. Age is not one. Redo the O11 card.
Eponyms are partly secure. Anchor Cushing to the brain and keep Kehr with splenic rupture. Redo the O12 card.
You swapped the walls at first, then held the pairing. Under pressure the labels can flip back: ask what lies behind the wall (free peritoneum in front, gastroduodenal artery behind).
You first read 'most common' as 'always', then corrected it. Under time pressure the word drops out again. Check for a non-ulcer cause of free gas.
You first diagnosed by location, then switched to checking haustra and the patient. Re-check this when a right-dome film looks classic.
You first used one ranking for every test question, then split first from best. Ask which question the stem poses each time.
You first gave one answer for both frames, then separated them. Name the frame before answering, especially on exam keys.
You first read no gas as no perforation, then corrected. Under pressure this habit returns; with peritonitis signs and a clear film, think CT.
You first picked a habitual view, then derived the right one. Re-derive it from where gas rises when the patient cannot sit.
You first assumed gas rises at once, then fixed the timing. Remember the mechanism: gas needs about 10 minutes upright to reach the diaphragm.
You first put surgery ahead of fluids, then re-ordered. Under exam pressure the definitive step tends to jump the queue; resuscitate first.
You first applied Taylor to a stable patient, then added the condition. Ask each time: sealed, confirmed on contrast, and selected?
You first treated the two patch names as interchangeable, then separated them. Keep both in mind: PYQs key Graham's patch, strictly Cellan-Jones is pedicled.
You first reached for vagotomy or gastrectomy, then switched. Older PYQs still list them; current practice is patch plus eradication and PPI.
You first swapped the pair, then fixed it. Anchor it: Cushing goes with the brain, Curling with burns.
You first followed the shared shoulder-tip pain to the wrong eponym, then corrected. Ask which disease owns each eponym.
You first read the lull as recovery, then fixed it. Late presenters who look better are the ones who catch people out; the lull comes before bacterial peritonitis.
You first reversed the movement sign, then traced the mechanism. Movement jars an inflamed peritoneum, whereas colic eases with moving.
You first closed a gastric ulcer like a duodenal one, then added the biopsy. Keep it as a cue when the stem mentions weight loss.
You first reached for barium, then switched. Ask what the medium does in the peritoneum.
You first added extra mortality factors or borrowed thresholds, then rebuilt it. Three items: shock, major illness, delay.
You first trusted a soft abdomen, then recognised masking. Elderly or steroid-treated patients may never show board-like rigidity.

You tend to match look-alikes by surface cues such as position or familiarity: wall, dome, contrast. For each pair, ask what actually differs, such as what lies behind, inside versus outside bowel, or what leaks.
You tend to turn a frequency or a test result into an absolute: most common into always, no gas into no perforation. Look for the qualifier and ask for a counter-case.
You tend to give one answer where the exam key and current practice differ. Name the frame in the stem first: PYQs expected one thing, current practice may favour another.
You tend to drop the qualifier that changes the answer: setting, host or condition. Before answering, ask which condition makes this the right choice.
You tend to put the definitive step first, or to leave out the step that depends on the case. Order the steps by what keeps the patient safe, then add case-specific steps.
You tend to map eponyms by a shared symptom or order of appearance. Anchor each eponym to the disease that owns it.
You tend to reverse the direction of a disease or sign: relief read as recovery, or movement read the wrong way. Predict the mechanism first, then check the sign.

You tapped Sure on at least two answers that were wrong. Those confident errors are the ones most worth correcting, so do their cards first. Before you tap Sure, name the qualifier that makes your answer right.
You asked for hints or explanations often. That is fine while the material is new, but it means some right answers had help. Retry the review cards without hints to see what you hold unaided.

Start the review cards with confident errors, then gaps, then shaky objectives. For each, find the qualifier or contrast the stem tests: first versus best, sealed versus free, exam key versus current practice. Revisit in 1 day, then 3 days.
